title: Samburu Meat Stew
author: Mama Wanjiru

heritage.origin: Samburu County and surrounding areas — Northern Kenya
heritage.history: The Samburu people are closely related to the Maasai and share a similar pastoralist culture. Their meat stew — slow-cooked in a clay pot with the animal's own fat — reflects the resourceful, direct approach to cooking of communities adapted to challenging environments.
heritage.modernEvolution: The Samburu meat stew tradition continues largely unchanged in rural communities.

desc: Samburu Meat Stew — bone-in goat or beef slow-simmered in a clay pot with onions, wild herbs, and the animal's own fat until deeply tender and richly flavoured. The traditional one-pot meal of the Samburu pastoralist community.
longDesc: Samburu meat stew is the daily sustenance of a community adapted to Northern Kenya's semi-arid conditions. Slow-simmered in clay pots over open fires, the meat cooks in its own juices with minimal additions.
ingredients: 1.5 kg bone-in goat or beef — cut into large pieces
2 tbsp animal fat or vegetable oil
steps: Heat fat in a clay pot or heavy casserole.
Brown the meat in batches over high heat.
Add garlic, salt, pepper, and herbs.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest simmer.
Cook covered for 75—90 minutes until the meat is completely tender.
chefTips: Clay pot cooking imparts a mineral character — use a clay casserole if possible.
The meat should be barely simmering.
The resulting broth is as important as the meat.
cookingScience: Clay pots are porous and allow slow, even heat distribution with slight moisture evaporation — creating a gentler cooking environment than metal pots.
sustainabilityTips: The Samburu pastoralist system sustainably manages cattle in Northern Kenya.
storage: Refrigerate for up to 4 days. Freeze for 3 months.
healthBenefits: Rich in collagen from bone-in cuts.
culturalNote: The Samburu meat stew tradition embodies the resourceful beauty of pastoralist cooking — maximum flavour from minimal ingredients.
